name: Guajona
body:
Guajona
CR 3

This thin, humanoid figure has wrinkled, yellow skin and bird-like taloned feet, with knots of thorny brambles in place of hands and a single long, curving fang stretching down almost to its chin.

XP 800
NE Medium aberration
Init +3; Senses darkvision 60 ft.; Perception +7

DEFENSE

AC 15, touch 13, flat-footed 12 (+3 Dex, +2 natural)
hp 32 (5d8+10)
Fort +5, Ref +5, Will +5; Weaknesses vulnerability to fire

OFFENSE

Speed 40 ft.
Melee curved fang +6 (1d6+3 plus anesthetic spittle) or claw +5 (1d4+3 slashing plus grab)
Space 5 ft.; Reach 5 ft.
Special Attacks snatching brambles

STATISTICS

Str 16, Dex 17, Con 14, Int 12, Wis 13, Cha 3
Base Atk +3; CMB +6 (+10 grapple); CMD 19
Feats Ability focus (anesthetic spittle), improved grapple
Skills Stealth +9, Survival +7
Languages Common, Aklo

SPECIAL ABILITIES

Anesthetic Spittle (Ex)

Curved fang—injury; save Fort DC 16; frequency 1/round for 6 rounds; effect 1d2 Str and 1d2 Dex; cure 1 save. The save DC is Constitution-based and includes the +2 bonus from Ability Focus.

Burns in Sunlight (Ex)

When a guajona ends its turn in direct sunlight, it bursts into flames, taking 1d6 points of fire damage and taking a -20 penalty on Stealth checks until the end of its next turn. Ending a turn out of the sun quenches the flames.

Snatching Brambles (Ex)

As a standard action, the guajona can stretch its bramble-claws out to make a claw attack against a target within 30 feet. If the guajona successfully grapples a Medium or smaller target, the target gains the grappled condition but the guajona does not (though she cannot make other claw attacks as long as it maintains the grapple). If the target is Medium or smaller, the guajona can make a second grapple maneuver as a free action against the same target; if it succeeds, the creature is pulled 10 feet toward the guajona.

ECOLOGY

Environment caves and urban areas
Organization solitary
Treasure incidental

This nocturnal creature is often mistaken for a hag or vampire but related to neither, though it is a hematophage, feeding on the blood of living humanoids. While humanoid in form, her taloned feet are inhuman, and even more so her hands.

Rather than flesh, strands of thorny brambles protrude from her wrists, twining together into an approximation of fingers. The eyes of a guajona shine with an inner light, and her most prominent facial feature is a single long, curving fang that descends down over the lower lip, coming to a point near the chin.

A guajona spends the daylight hours burrowed under the ground or in a convenient cave or abandoned building. Exposure to sunlight immediately begins to burn the guajona’s skin, and prolonged exposure causes death.

At night, the guajona comes forth to hunt.

The guajona’s saliva is a powerful anesthetic, deadening sensation upon contact. When hunting, the guajona typically picks a sleeping victim, anesthetizing an area on their body before biting in with its tooth and draining blood from the victim. The guajona places the bite in a place not easily seen, to hide evidence of its attack. Often the victim is assumed to be ill, becoming more tired and drained as the guajona feeds on consecutive nights, until the victim dies.
